issues.legal_issue: A court may add or alter an offence charge, and omission to frame a charge does not by itself invalidate a conviction where the accused knew the case to meet and suffered no failure of justice or actual prejudice.
material_facts: The trial court found that two accused had caused injuries to the deceased but did not convict them for those injuries because the corresponding charges had not been framed.
The accused had also been charged with murder jointly, and the trial court considered their participation in the assault.

The Supreme Court held that the trial court could have added or altered charges and proceeded according to law; it was not justified in treating the absence of charges in the police charge-sheet as preventing conviction for an offence supported by the evidence.
issues.conclusion: The trial court erred in declining to proceed on the offences supported by the evidence merely because the corresponding charges had not been framed. An omitted or defective charge does not invalidate a conviction unless it caused a failure of justice, including actual prejudice to the accused.
issues.legal_principle: Section 216 CrPC empowers a trial court to alter or add a charge before the conclusion of trial; Section 217 permits recall of witnesses where required after such alteration or addition. Appellate courts may exercise charge-altering powers under Sections 385(2) and 386 CrPC. Under Sections 464 and 465 CrPC, omission or irregularity in a charge does not invalidate a conviction unless it has occasioned a failure of justice. The court must assess whether the accused understood the case and had a full and fair opportunity to defend it. The Court relied on Hasanbhai Valibhai Qureshi v. State of Gujarat, Kantilal Chandulal Mehta v. State of Maharashtra, Amar Singh v. State of Haryana, Sanichar Sahni v. State of Bihar, and the authorities discussed in those decisions.

rule.if: criminal_case_with_omitted_charge and evidence_supports_offense and accused_understood_case and defense_opportunity and not actual_prejudice

predicates.criminal_case_with_omitted_charge: A criminal trial or appeal concerns an offence for which no charge was framed or the charge was defective.
predicates.evidence_supports_offense: The evidence presented in the case supports the offence for which no charge was framed.
predicates.accused_understood_case: The accused was informed, through the charges and proceedings, of the substance of the case against them.
predicates.defense_opportunity: The accused had a full and fair opportunity to defend against the facts said to establish the offence.
predicates.actual_prejudice: The omission or defect caused the accused a real disadvantage in the investigation or trial or otherwise caused a failure of justice.

issues.definition: When a criminal case includes an omitted charge, the evidence supports the offence, and the accused understood and could defend against the case without actual prejudice, the omission alone does not invalidate a conviction for that offence.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court cannot sustain a murder conviction based on common intention merely because the accused were charged jointly when it leaves undisturbed a finding that they did not share the relevant common intention.
material_facts: The trial court found that the accused did not act in furtherance of a common intention and convicted two of them only of lesser offences.
The High Court convicted those two accused of murder read with common intention because they had been charged under that provision.
The High Court did not reverse the trial court’s finding that the accused had not shared a common intention to cause the relevant grievous injuries.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s conclusion that the two accused were guilty of murder read with common intention was not justified because it left undisturbed the finding that they had not acted in furtherance of a common intention.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34 IPC requires criminal liability for a joint act to rest on a common intention shared by the participants; the existence of a charge alone does not establish that element. The Supreme Court applied this principle to the High Court’s appellate decision, which had not displaced the trial court’s finding on common intention.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_reviewing_joint_murder_conviction and lower_court_found_no_common_intention and appellate_court_left_finding_undisturbed and charge_alone_used_to_convict

predicates.criminal_appeal_reviewing_joint_murder_c: An appellate court is reviewing a murder conviction imposed on multiple accused through a joint-liability theory.
predicates.lower_court_found_no_common_intention: The lower court found that the accused did not share the common intention required for joint liability.
predicates.appellate_court_left_finding_undisturbed: The appellate court did not reverse or displace the lower court’s finding that common intention was absent.
predicates.charge_alone_used_to_convict: The appellate court relied on the fact that the accused had been charged jointly, without establishing the required common intention.

issues.definition: When an appellate court leaves undisturbed a finding that common intention was absent, the fact that the accused were charged jointly does not justify a joint murder conviction.

issues.legal_issue: A spontaneous fatal assault arising from a heated exchange, without premeditation or an intent to kill, may warrant conviction for culpable homicide not amounting to murder rather than murder.
material_facts: The fatal assault arose after a heated exchange over use of land and occurred in the spur of the moment rather than as a premeditated attack.
The accused used agricultural implements during the assault, and the deceased suffered multiple injuries, including injuries that caused his death.
The accused stopped assaulting the deceased after he fell and left the scene.
The Supreme Court concluded that the accused did not intend to kill the deceased and that the circumstances supported liability for culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
issues.conclusion: The Court set aside the murder convictions and convicted all three accused under Section 304 Part I read with Section 34 IPC, while maintaining their convictions under Sections 447 and 504 IPC.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Sections 304 Part I and 34 IPC to the fatal assault, finding that the circumstances showed a spontaneous incident without a premeditated intent to kill, while the accused participated in the assault together. It did not rely on an earlier case for this conclusion.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_murder_conviction and multiple_accused_participated_in_fatal_assault and fatal_assault_followed_spontaneous_quarrel and assault_stopped_after_victim_fell and not premeditated_intent_to_kill

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_murder_conviction: A criminal appeal concerns a conviction for murder arising from a fatal assault.
predicates.multiple_accused_participated_in_fatal_a: More than one accused participated in the assault that caused the death.
predicates.fatal_assault_followed_spontaneous_quarr: The fatal assault followed a sudden quarrel or heated exchange rather than a planned attack.
predicates.assault_stopped_after_victim_fell: The assailants stopped the assault after the victim fell.
predicates.premeditated_intent_to_kill: The fatal assault was planned in advance with an intent to kill the victim.

issues.definition: When multiple accused participate in a fatal assault that follows a spontaneous quarrel, stops after the victim falls, and is not premeditated with an intent to kill, the ruling is culpable homicide not amounting to murder with joint liability.
